title: Business Strategy: How Firms Compete
description: How firms choose where and how to compete, and how a learner judges those choices: which force holds an industry's profit down, whether an advantage can be copied, whether to make or buy, and why an incumbent missed a shift. Australian cases throughout, from supermarkets and airlines to Wesfarmers, Atlassian and Canva.
audience: A capable adult who has met supply, demand, monopoly and game theory, can read a margin in an annual report, and wants to judge a firm's strategic choices with real cases in front of them. No finance or management study is assumed.
outcomes: You'll be able to tell a strategy from an objective and test whether a claimed trade-off is real.
You'll be able to say which of the five forces holds an industry's profit down and why a firm in it may still do better or worse than its rivals.
You'll be able to judge which obstacles to entry are real barriers and how much bargaining power a buyer or supplier has.
You'll be able to name the position a firm has chosen, test an advantage with VRIO and read where in a firm's chain the profit sits.
You'll be able to say whether a market will tip, how tied in its customers are, and which pricing approach fits.
You'll be able to apply three tests to a diversification, and judge whether a firm should make or buy.
You'll be able to explain why a good incumbent misses a disruptive shift, judge first-mover and price-war moves, and diagnose why a plan failed.

modules.title: Strategy and the industry
modules.summary: What strategy is, and how the shape of an industry decides how much profit its firms can keep: the five forces, entry barriers and bargaining power.

modules.title: Advantage inside the firm
modules.summary: How a firm earns more than its rivals: cost, differentiation and focus, resources that rivals cannot copy, and the part of the chain where profit sits.

modules.title: Networks, lock-in and price
modules.summary: Why some markets tip to one firm, how customers get tied in, and how pricing builds or hides all of it.

lessons.title: What strategy is
lessons.objective: Tell a strategy, which is a chosen position with trade-offs and activities that fit, from an objective or a tactic, and judge whether a claimed trade-off is real and whether an advantage will last.

concepts.title: Strategy
concepts.summary: A chosen position in an industry, made real by trade-offs about what the firm will not do and by activities that fit together (Porter's three principles).

concepts.title: Trade-off
concepts.summary: A choice that excludes another. It is real when matching it would cost a rival something, and false when it only hides weak execution.

concepts.title: Objective and strategy
concepts.summary: An objective says what the firm wants (a satisfactory return); a strategy says how it will compete to get it.

concepts.title: Sustainable advantage
concepts.summary: An edge rivals cannot copy quickly or cheaply, which is what lets a firm earn more than the average in its industry.

concepts.title: Emergent strategy
concepts.summary: The part of what a firm actually does that no plan set out, formed by decisions made along the way.

misconceptions: That a strategy is an ambition or a target. 'Satisfactory return to shareholders' is an objective; it says nothing about how the firm competes.
That a strategy is everything a firm does. The choices that define a strategy include what it refuses to do, as in Virgin Australia's 'we won't be either'.
That trade-offs are always real. A firm that says it cannot offer quality and low cost may only be showing that its own operations are weaker than a rival's.
That any advantage counts. A promotion that a rival can copy by Friday is not a sustained advantage.
sequence: Open on Virgin Australia's 2020 sentence about being neither a low-cost nor a full-service airline, and ask what it commits the firm to and what it gives up (s1_virgin, s1_virgin_context, s1_virgin_effect).
Give Porter's three principles and Rumelt's kernel as ways of checking a statement: position, trade-offs, fit; diagnosis, guiding policy, coherent actions (s1_porter3, s1_rumelt, s1_limited).
Set Wesfarmers' one-line objective beside its separate 'value-creating strategies' to show that an objective is not a strategy (s1_wes_objective).
Real and false trade-offs: Qantas runs two brands so that each can make its own trade-offs (s1_dual, s1_jetstar_why); the book's Lexus case shows a false one (s1_tradeoff).
Why an advantage lasts: the coffee shop whose special is copied at once against the one whose atmosphere took years to build (s1_coffee), and why firms chase above-average returns (s1_aar).
Close on emergence: what a firm ends up doing is its plan plus what emerged, and emergence matters more when the world is hard to forecast (s1_emergent).
examples: Virgin Australia, November 2020: 'Australia already has a low-cost carrier and a traditional full-service airline, and we won't be either' (ACCC, 2023). What followed: one aircraft type, no complimentary meals, fewer regional routes it could serve itself.
Qantas Group: Qantas as the full-service brand and Jetstar as the budget leisure brand, together about 60% of domestic passengers (ACCC).
Invented, labelled as such: a bank that says low fees and fast service cannot go together while a rival offers both.

figures.shows: A three-row card for Virgin Australia's 2020 sentence: what it commits to, what it gives up, what had to change (fleet, onboard offer). Cells filled from the ACCC extract.
figures.learnerAction: Drag each consequence the ACCC lists to the row it belongs in.

figures.learnerAction: Tick one column per statement.

questionPlan.sample: Sort each statement into Objective, Strategic choice (it commits the firm to a position and excludes another) or Tactic. (1) 'To provide a satisfactory return to shareholders' (Wesfarmers). (2) 'Australia already has a low-cost carrier and a traditional full-service airline, and we won't be either' (Virgin Australia). (3) A two-for-one coffee special this week (invented). (4) Qantas runs Jetstar as a separate budget leisure brand beside its full-service brand. (5) 'Become the market leader in hardware' (invented).
questionPlan.answer: Objective: 1 and 5. Strategic choice: 2 and 4. Tactic: 3.
questionPlan.why: Item 5 sounds strategic but names a result, not a way to compete; item 3 can be copied at once.

questionPlan.sample: Virgin Australia's chief executive said in 2020 that 'Australia already has a low-cost carrier and a traditional full-service airline, and we won't be either'. Which reading is best?
questionPlan.answer: A position defined partly by what Virgin will not be, with consequences for how it operates
choices: A target to grow faster than both rivals, which names a result and not a way of competing
A slogan that changes nothing about how the airline is run, since all airlines sell seats
A position defined partly by what Virgin will not be, with consequences for how it operates
questionPlan.why: First wrong option confuses a goal with a choice. Third ignores what the ACCC records: no complimentary meals, one fleet type, less regional reach.

questionPlan.sample: A bank says it cannot give low fees and fast service together because they trade off. A rival gives both on the same products by running a simpler process. What does that show? (Both banks are invented.)
questionPlan.answer: That the first bank's trade-off was false: its higher cost came from how it works
choices: That the first bank's trade-off was false: its higher cost came from how it works
That the rival must be losing money on each customer, since nobody can offer both for long
That trade-offs never exist in any business, since a clever enough process removes every one
questionPlan.why: First: an assumption nothing in the case supports. Second: over-corrects; real trade-offs exist where activities or images conflict.

questionPlan.sample: Café A draws crowds with a half-price special. Café B draws them with baristas it has trained for years and a fit-out its rivals cannot easily get. Which advantage is more likely to last, and why? (Both cafés are invented.)
questionPlan.answer: B's, because a rival can copy a price cut at once but must spend time and money to copy people and place
choices: A's, because customers always choose the lower price and a special reaches them at once
B's, because a rival can copy a price cut at once but must spend time and money to copy people and place
Both, because any advantage that draws customers away from rivals lasts as long as it draws them
questionPlan.why: First treats price as the only thing customers weigh. Third ignores that lasting depends on how costly the copy is.

questionPlan.sample: A cable channel was planned to cover sport in one state, then grew into a national network because its early success opened options nobody had planned. What term does the lesson use for the part of its strategy that no plan set out?
questionPlan.answer: Emergent strategy (accept 'emergent')

questionPlan.sample: Without looking back, state Porter's three principles of strategy and say which one a slogan most often leaves out.
questionPlan.answer: Self-rated: a unique and valuable position; trade-offs by choosing what not to do; fit among activities. Slogans most often leave out the trade-offs.

lessons.title: The five forces
lessons.objective: Use the five forces to say which force holds an industry's profit down, and keep that separate from why one firm in the industry earns more than another.

concepts.title: The five forces
concepts.summary: Rivalry, new entrants, substitutes, buyer power and supplier power: the pressures that decide how much of an industry's value its firms keep.

concepts.title: Rivalry
concepts.summary: How hard existing firms compete. With few large rivals who watch each other, a price cut is matched and nobody gains share.

concepts.title: Substitute
concepts.summary: A product that meets the same need by a different route, such as video calls for business flights.

concepts.title: Industry profit and firm profit
concepts.summary: The forces describe how much profit an industry can earn; which firm takes it depends on that firm's own position.

misconceptions: That a concentrated industry makes every firm profitable. Virgin Australia sat in a duopoly and still went into administration in 2020.
That any competitor is a substitute. A substitute meets the same need a different way; a new airline is a rival or entrant.
That the forces tell you which firm will win. The Qantas Group took by its own estimate about 90% of domestic industry profit in FY2015 to FY2019: the pool and its owner are different questions.
That a few large rivals fight hard on price. The ACCC finds Coles and Woolworths have little incentive to beat each other on it.
sequence: Start from the ACCC's grocery numbers: shares of 38%, 29%, 9% and 7%, high barriers, and the finding of limited incentive to compete on price (s2_aldi_shares, s2_not_close, s2_85pct).
Why two big rivals do not cut prices: a cut is matched, so the margin falls and no share is won (s2_oligopoly_logic, s2_oligopoly).
Name the five forces and the horizontal and vertical split (s2_def, s2_horiz), then separate substitutes from rivals (s2_substitute) and note how buyer alternatives set buyer power (s2_buyer).
ALDI as the one constraint, and only where its range overlaps (s2_aldi_constraint).
Airlines: the same duopoly logic (s2_air_duopoly, s2_air_9in10), the early-2010s price war when it broke down (s2_air_price_war), and the quiet years after (s2_air_content).
Who takes the profit: the Qantas Group share of industry EBIT (s2_air_profits) and the industry-versus-firm split of profit in the research Morris and Tripathi report (s2_industry_firm).
A substitute at work: online technology replacing some business travel (s2_air_substitute).
examples: ACCC: Woolworths 38%, Coles 29%, ALDI 9%, Metcash 7% of supermarket grocery sales; supermarkets about 85% of grocery spend, Coles and Woolworths two-thirds of supermarket sales.
ACCC: since 2002 over 9 in 10 domestic passengers have flown Qantas or Virgin groups; Qantas Group about 70% of industry EBIT in FY2011-15 and about 90% in FY2015-19, by its own estimate.
Early 2010s: both airlines added capacity and cut fares; the price war was unsustainable and both lost heavily.

figures.shows: Five ACCC findings about Australian grocery in one column, five force names across the top.
figures.learnerAction: Place each finding under the force it describes.

figures.shows: Domestic airline competition from 2002 to 2023 with three marked periods: Ansett's end and the duopoly, the early-2010s price war, the content years. No profit figures are shown.
figures.learnerAction: Mark each period as intense or muted rivalry, then reveal the ACCC's description.

questionPlan.sample: Which force does each ACCC finding about grocery describe? Rivalry, New entrants, Substitutes or Buyer power. (1) Coles and Woolworths face no rivals of comparable scope and scale. (2) There are significant barriers to entry and expansion at large scale. (3) Butchers, greengrocers, Costco and online marketplaces can supply part of a shopper's basket. (4) Convenience matters most and comparing prices takes time, so most shoppers do not split their main shop across stores.
questionPlan.answer: 1 Rivalry; 2 New entrants; 3 Substitutes; 4 Buyer power.
questionPlan.why: Item 3 is a different route to the same need; item 4 is the weak power of buyers, which keeps rivalry mild.

questionPlan.sample: The ACCC reports that the Qantas Group earned by its own estimate about 70% of domestic airline industry EBIT in FY2011-15 and about 90% in FY2015-19. What can the five forces not tell you about this?
questionPlan.answer: Which firm in the industry will take the profit the industry earns
choices: Whether the industry has a few large rivals who watch each other's prices
Which firm in the industry will take the profit the industry earns
Whether new entrants face barriers that protect the profit the industry earns
questionPlan.why: The first and third are what the forces are for. The second is a firm-level question, answered by resources and position.

questionPlan.sample: In the early 2010s Virgin Blue became Virgin Australia and went after Qantas's corporate customers. Both airlines added seats and cut fares, then abandoned the fight after significant losses. Which force strengthened, and what did it do to profit?
questionPlan.answer: Rivalry, which pushed down the profit of both airlines
choices: Supplier power, which raised the airlines' costs and so cut the profit of both
Buyer power, because passengers organised and forced both airlines to cut fares
Rivalry, which pushed down the profit of both airlines
questionPlan.why: The case gives no supplier-cost story and no organised buyers; it gives a fight for share between two rivals.

questionPlan.sample: A video-conference service lets companies skip some interstate trips, and a new airline starts flying Sydney to Melbourne. Which is the substitute for a business flight? (The airline is real; the framing is the lesson's.)
questionPlan.answer: The video-conference service, because it meets the need by a different route
choices: The new airline, because it competes for the same passengers on the same route
The video-conference service, because it meets the need by a different route
Neither, because a substitute only exists for cheap goods that buyers can drop
questionPlan.why: A same-technology rival is a rival or an entrant; the ACCC itself notes online technology replacing some business travel.

questionPlan.sample: Source A: the ACCC calls the Australian domestic airline industry a duopoly, one of the most highly concentrated outside natural monopolies. Source B: Virgin Australia went into voluntary administration in April 2020 with significant levels of debt. What do the two together show?
questionPlan.answer: Concentration does not make every firm profitable; what a firm earns also depends on its own position and choices
choices: Concentration does not make every firm profitable; what a firm earns also depends on its own position and choices
Concentration has no effect on profit, since Virgin lost money despite a duopoly and nothing else matters
Virgin's trouble was caused by COVID alone, so it says nothing about the firm's position or its debt
questionPlan.why: First over-corrects. Second ignores the debt and the earlier price war the ACCC describes. (Source B states the administration, not its cause.)

questionPlan.sample: Name the five forces and say which three are 'horizontal' and which two 'vertical'.
questionPlan.answer: Self-rated: rivalry, new entrants, substitutes (horizontal); supplier power, buyer power (vertical).

lessons.title: Barriers to entry and bargaining power
lessons.objective: Judge which obstacles are real barriers to entry, weigh conflicting claims about them, and say how much power a buyer or supplier has from its alternatives and its share of the other side's business.

concepts.title: Barrier to entry
concepts.summary: A cost an entrant must bear that incumbents do not or did not have to (Stigler, Baumol and Willig).

concepts.title: Sunk entry cost
concepts.summary: Money spent to enter that cannot be recovered if entry fails, which raises the stakes of a wrong bet.

concepts.title: Buyer power
concepts.summary: Rises with the alternatives buyers have and with the share of a supplier's output they take.

concepts.title: Monopsony power
concepts.summary: A buyer large enough to affect the market price, which the ACCC finds most often for perishable fresh produce.

misconceptions: That a large investment is by itself a barrier. The ACCC finds capital is not a barrier for large international entrants, though sunk cost raises the stakes.
That a barrier is permanent. ALDI entered in 2001 and took more than 20 years to reach its position.
That the largest buyer has power over every supplier. Power depends on alternatives and share: Metcash's IGA stores buy most fresh produce elsewhere.
That an entrant's or an incumbent's account of a barrier settles it. Each has a stake in how it describes the barrier.
sequence: Define a barrier as a cost the entrant bears and the incumbent does not (s3_stigler, s3_baumol) and list Porter's sources (s3_porter_switch, s3_primary).
The ACCC's four conditions for large-scale supermarket entry and the 20-year ALDI timeline (s3_entry_needs, s3_aldi_20).
Two accounts of supplier networks, from ALDI and from Woolworths, and how the ACCC weighs them with its own view (s3_aldi_supplier, s3_woolies_supplier, s3_supplier_net_acc).
Capital and sunk cost: Kaufland's roughly $500m, about $300m unrecovered (s3_capital, s3_kaufland); sites and land banking (s3_sites, s3_landbank).
Airlines: reputation, crew, aircraft, regulation, and the legacy and slots behind Qantas's position (s3_air_barriers, s3_air_legacy, s3_air_slots).

Bargaining power: buyer power and alternatives (s2_buyer); fresh produce as the case where the chains' power is strongest (s3_monopsony_def, s3_monopsony_factors, s3_aldi_fresh, s3_info) and where buyer power can lower prices (s3_buyer_power_good).
The other side of the chain: independents depend on Metcash for some packaged lines, and not for fresh (s3_metcash_little, s3_metcash_74, s3_metcash_fresh).
examples: ACCC: ALDI entered in 2001 and took more than 20 years to reach its position; the two chains hold more than 150 undeveloped sites.
Kaufland: about $500m invested, about $300m unrecovered, per the ACCC's estimate from ASIC filings.
Metcash estimates about 74% of IGA purchases go through it, and IGA stores source 50 to 90% of fresh groceries elsewhere.

figures.shows: Four supermarket entry factors, each with the ACCC's verdict hidden and a short list of what ALDI, Woolworths and the ACCC said.
figures.learnerAction: Rate each factor as a significant barrier or not, then reveal the ACCC's view.

figures.shows: A line from 'many alternatives' to 'few alternatives' with Metcash's packaged groceries and fresh produce placed from the ACCC text.
figures.learnerAction: Place each case on the line before the labels appear.

questionPlan.sample: For large-scale entry into Australian supermarkets, sort each factor by the ACCC's view: Significant barrier, or Less significant or not a barrier. (1) Access to suitable retail sites. (2) Economies of scale at the wholesale level. (3) Building a supplier network. (4) Access to capital, for large well-established international retailers.
questionPlan.answer: Significant barrier: 1 and 2. Less significant or not a barrier: 3 and 4.
questionPlan.why: Items 3 and 4 are the two where entrants and incumbents disagreed; the ACCC weighs both and finds neither the main barrier.

questionPlan.sample: Source A, ALDI: when it entered it was unknown to suppliers and had to find those willing to take a chance. Source B, Woolworths: suppliers always look to sell across a range of retailers and happily offer ranges to Amazon and Woolworths. What matters most in weighing them?
questionPlan.answer: Each speaker's stake: ALDI was the entrant and Woolworths the incumbent, so each describes the barrier in the way that suits it
choices: Woolworths is right, because the larger firm has more data on how suppliers behave toward every retailer
ALDI is right, because it entered and succeeded, so supplier networks cannot be much of a barrier
Each speaker's stake: ALDI was the entrant and Woolworths the incumbent, so each describes the barrier in the way that suits it
questionPlan.why: First treats size as truth. Second is survivorship: one success says little about the entrants who did not appear.

questionPlan.sample: Kaufland invested about $500m in Australian entry, of which about $300m was unrecovered, per the ACCC. What does that show about entry barriers?
questionPlan.answer: That sunk cost raises the price of a wrong bet, so entrants must be surer than the capital figure alone suggests
choices: That sunk cost raises the price of a wrong bet, so entrants must be surer than the capital figure alone suggests
That capital is the main barrier for every entrant, so a larger fund always wins entry
That Kaufland was badly managed, since an entrant that loses money has made avoidable mistakes
questionPlan.why: First contradicts the ACCC's finding for large international retailers. Second is not in the source.

questionPlan.sample: IGA retailers buy about 74% of what they stock through Metcash but source 50 to 90% of fresh groceries elsewhere. What does that say about Metcash's bargaining power over an IGA store?
questionPlan.answer: Strong on some packaged lines where stores lack choice, weak on fresh where they have many suppliers
choices: Strong on everything, because Metcash is the largest wholesaler to independent stores
Strong on some packaged lines where stores lack choice, weak on fresh where they have many suppliers
Weak on everything, because each store is locally owned and can walk away at any time
questionPlan.why: Power depends on the alternatives for each line, not on the supplier's size overall.

questionPlan.sample: A new airline faces fuel and wage costs that Qantas also faces, and it faces a slot allocation that the ACCC says gives incumbents a preference. Which is the barrier to entry? (The airline is invented.)
questionPlan.answer: The slot allocation, because Qantas does not bear that cost in the same way
choices: The fuel and wage costs, because they are the largest costs a new airline will face
Neither, because airlines are protected by regulation and so face no barriers at all
The slot allocation, because Qantas does not bear that cost in the same way
questionPlan.why: A cost both bear is not a barrier however large; the ACCC identifies incumbency advantages and slot access.

questionPlan.sample: State the test for a barrier to entry in one sentence, then give one cost that is large but is not a barrier.
questionPlan.answer: Self-rated: a cost the entrant bears that the incumbent does not (or did not) bear. A cost both bear, such as fuel, is large but not a barrier.

lessons.title: Cost, differentiation and focus
lessons.objective: Name the position a firm has chosen from what it does, check whether its activities fit it, and say what the position costs.

concepts.title: Cost leadership
concepts.summary: Winning on the lowest price in a market by keeping costs lower than rivals, through utilisation, standard no-frills products and tight control of the chain.

concepts.title: Differentiation
concepts.summary: Charging more because customers value something other than price, such as quality or service.

concepts.title: Focus
concepts.summary: Serving one or a few segments, either at lower cost or with a differentiated offer.

concepts.title: Stuck in the middle
concepts.summary: Porter's warning that a firm trying to be everything has no distinct advantage; later research finds some firms combine low cost and differentiation.

misconceptions: That low prices alone make a cost leader. A cost position needs the activities that produce low cost, such as narrow range and no online delivery.
That moving up-market is free. Virgin Blue's move into business travel brought it into direct competition with Qantas and a price war.
That a combination is always a mistake. Wikipedia reports research that firms combining low cost and differentiation may do better than those that pick one.
That a second brand is just a discount tier. A separate brand lets each position keep its own activities.
sequence: Porter's three generic strategies and the two axes of advantage and scope (s4_gs, s4_gs_cost); what a cost leader does (s4_cost_assets) and what it risks (s4_cost_risk).

ALDI as a worked case: roughly 1,800 to 2,000 products against 15,000 to 25,000, narrower range, own brands, no online (s4_aldi_range, s4_aldi_limits, s4_aldi_no_online) and a refusal of loyalty programs that kept the cost position (s4_aldi_loyalty, s4_aldi_share).
Virgin Blue's formula and its 2011 move up-market (s4_blue_formula, s4_blue_rebrand, s4_blue_transition) and the 2020 'middle' position (s1_virgin, s1_virgin_effect).
The stuck-in-the-middle claim and the later evidence against it (s4_stuck, s4_both, s4_hybrid).
Two brands in one group: Qantas and Jetstar, with Qantas's own claim about margins (s1_dual, s1_jetstar_why, s4_qan_dual).
A group-level cost story: Kmart's private label and low pricing, and Wesfarmers linking low prices to low costs (s4_kmart, s4_wes_cost).
examples: ALDI: about 1,800 to 2,000 products in about 1,000 m2 against 15,000 to 25,000 in 1,500 to 4,000 m2 at Coles and Woolworths; national share from 2.8% in 2006-07 to 8.1% in 2022-23 (ACCC).
Virgin Blue: no included meals, one aircraft type, limited airports; 2011 rebrand to attract business travellers.
Qantas FY26: Group Domestic margin 13%, a company claim attributed to its dual brand strategy.

figures.shows: Two columns, 'ALDI' and 'Coles and Woolworths', with rows for range, floor area, brands, online and loyalty program, values from the ACCC.
figures.learnerAction: Mark each cell as cost-driven or offer-driven.

figures.shows: A map with price level on one axis and breadth of service on the other, with Jetstar, Qantas and Virgin Australia (2011 and 2020) as movable pins.
figures.learnerAction: Place each pin, then compare with the ACCC description.

questionPlan.sample: Which of these ALDI features fit a low-cost position, and which belong to a full-range position? (1) About 1,800 to 2,000 products. (2) Mostly own brands. (3) 15,000 to 25,000 products. (4) No online shopping or delivery. (5) Stores of 1,500 to 4,000 m2.
questionPlan.answer: Low-cost: 1, 2, 4. Full-range: 3, 5.
questionPlan.why: Items 3 and 5 are Coles and Woolworths' figures.

questionPlan.sample: In 2011 Virgin Blue dropped 'Blue' to attract more business travellers from Qantas. How does the ACCC describe the result?
questionPlan.answer: It met Qantas head-on for corporate customers and a price war followed that proved unsustainable
choices: It escaped competition by serving a niche that Qantas had ignored for years
It met Qantas head-on for corporate customers and a price war followed that proved unsustainable
It became a cost leader, because adding business class lowered its unit costs
questionPlan.why: First reverses the finding. Third mistakes the move: business class is a differentiation feature.

questionPlan.sample: Virgin Australia after 2020 aimed at 'value-conscious' travellers in the middle, moved to one aircraft type, and dropped complimentary meals. What does the ACCC say this cost it?
questionPlan.answer: Less ability to serve some regional routes itself, though Qantas faces it less directly in premium corporate travel
choices: Less ability to serve some regional routes itself, though Qantas faces it less directly in premium corporate travel
Nothing, because a position in the middle of the market carries none of the trade-offs of either end
Its brand, because customers came to see the airline as low-cost and stopped paying for business travel
questionPlan.why: Every position has a cost; the ACCC names them. Third is not in the source.

questionPlan.sample: Why might Qantas run Jetstar as a separate brand rather than add low fares to the Qantas brand?
questionPlan.answer: Each position needs its own activities, and mixing them risks leaving both without a clear advantage
choices: Because competition law required Qantas to keep its budget flights in a separate company
Because low fares and full service cost the same to produce, so only the label differs
Each position needs its own activities, and mixing them risks leaving both without a clear advantage
questionPlan.why: First is not in the pack. Third is the opposite of the trade-off idea.

questionPlan.sample: ALDI says a loyalty program would add cost and complexity, and it has no program. Its national share rose from 2.8% in 2006-07 to 8.1% in 2022-23. What does the case show?
questionPlan.answer: A cost position is kept partly by refusing activities that add cost without adding to the low-price offer
choices: A cost position is kept partly by refusing activities that add cost without adding to the low-price offer
That loyalty programs cannot help any retailer, whatever its strategy
That ALDI's share would have grown faster if it had run a loyalty program like its rivals
questionPlan.why: First over-generalises from one case. Third needs evidence the pack does not give.

questionPlan.sample: Describe the three generic strategies and the later finding that complicates 'stuck in the middle'.
questionPlan.answer: Self-rated: cost leadership, differentiation, focus (cost or differentiation); later research suggests some firms combining low cost and differentiation do better than those pursuing one.

lessons.title: Resources and capabilities
lessons.objective: Test a claimed advantage with the four VRIO questions and say whether it is temporary parity or sustainable, and what the evidence can and cannot show.

concepts.title: VRIO
concepts.summary: Four questions about a resource or capability: is it valuable, rare, costly to imitate, and is the firm organised to capture its value.

concepts.title: Cost of imitation
concepts.summary: Why a rival cannot copy cheaply: unique history, causal ambiguity, social complexity, or patents.

concepts.title: Organised to capture value
concepts.summary: Having a valuable, rare resource is not enough without the structure and systems to exploit it.

concepts.title: Parity and temporary advantage
concepts.summary: A valuable thing that rivals can get as cheaply as you can gives no edge; if it is rare but copyable, the edge is temporary.

misconceptions: That a valuable resource is a sustained advantage. If every rival can get it at the same cost, it is only parity.
That rare means safe. A rare resource that can be copied or substituted gives a temporary advantage.

That owning the resource is enough. Kodak built the first self-contained digital camera prototype in the mid-1970s and still struggled with the shift; the question is whether the firm is organised to exploit it.
That a firm's own account shows its advantage is hard to copy. A description of how Atlassian sells does not say whether a rival could copy it.
sequence: The four VRIO questions (s5_vrio_q) and rarity needing persistence (s5_rarity); imitability as a cost question (s5_imit, s5_imit_form).
Why imitation is costly (s5_cost_imit) with the Qantas case: a legacy of routes, terminals and slots from the 1992 merger (s5_qan_legacy, s5_qan_adv, s3_air_legacy).
Qantas's loyalty program as a capability: 16.4 million members in June 2024 on one source, 18.9 million in FY26 on the company's own (s5_qff, s5_qan_loyalty).
The coffee shop again: copyable promotion against slow-to-copy people and place (s1_coffee).
Kodak as the case of a rare, valuable resource not turned into advantage (s11_kodak_invented, s11_kodak_myth).
Atlassian's land-and-expand distribution: what the 10-K says it does and why, and the question it leaves open (s5_atl_dist, s5_atl_wiki).
examples: Qantas: 'largest domestic route network, schedule, network of airport lounges, and customer loyalty program' as advantages (ACCC); program 16.4m members at June 2024 (Wikipedia); 18.9m members, $625m EBIT and 21.7% margin in FY26 (company).
Atlassian: self-service web purchasing with a direct sales force only for large customers (10-K).
Kodak: invented the first self-contained digital camera prototype in the mid-1970s and, by 2005, ranked first in US digital camera sales.

figures.shows: Four claimed advantages as rows (a promotion; Qantas's legacy of routes and slots; Qantas's loyalty program; Atlassian's online sales model), VRIO columns with 'known', 'not in the sources' and 'inferred' marks.
figures.learnerAction: Fill each cell, then see which the pack supports.

figures.shows: A decision path: valuable? rare? costly to imitate? organised? ending in disadvantage, parity, temporary advantage, unused advantage or sustained advantage.
figures.learnerAction: Walk each case down the path.

questionPlan.sample: The ACCC says Qantas benefited from its 1992 merger with Australian Airlines, one of only two airlines permitted to run domestic flights before liberalisation, giving it early routes and access to terminals and slots. Which reason for costly imitation does this best match?
questionPlan.answer: Unique historical conditions, because the access came with a moment in history that rivals cannot recreate
choices: Social complexity, because the advantage rests on culture and relationships among staff
Unique historical conditions, because the access came with a moment in history that rivals cannot recreate
Patents, because Qantas holds exclusive legal rights over its network
questionPlan.why: Social complexity would be culture and relationships; the ACCC describes access won at a moment that cannot recur.

questionPlan.sample: A firm holds a resource that is valuable and rare, but rivals can obtain it at no cost disadvantage. What does VRIO say it gives?
questionPlan.answer: A temporary advantage at most, because rivals can get the same resource without a cost disadvantage
choices: A sustained advantage, because anything valuable and rare will hold up against rivals
A temporary advantage at most, because rivals can get the same resource without a cost disadvantage
A permanent disadvantage, because rivals gain the same resource at no extra cost
questionPlan.why: First stops after two questions. Third mistakes parity for loss.

questionPlan.sample: Kodak developed the first self-contained digital camera prototype in the mid-1970s and still struggled with the move to digital. Which VRIO question best explains how a firm can hold a valuable, rare resource and not gain from it?
questionPlan.answer: Whether the firm was organised to capture the value
choices: Whether the resource was valuable to customers in the first place
Whether the resource was rare enough to be held only by Kodak
Whether the firm was organised to capture the value
questionPlan.why: The resource passed the first two questions; the article's point is that Kodak did not refuse to invest in digital.

questionPlan.sample: Atlassian's 10-K says it lands customers by web self-service and uses a direct sales force for large customers, which lowers acquisition cost. What can an analyst conclude about whether this is a sustained advantage?
questionPlan.answer: That it is valuable to Atlassian; whether rivals can copy it is not in the source and still has to be tested
choices: That it is valuable to Atlassian; whether rivals can copy it is not in the source and still has to be tested
That it is sustained, because Atlassian describes it as the core of its model and it has worked for years
That it is only parity, because every software company sells over the web in the same way
questionPlan.why: A firm's description is not a test of imitability. Third asserts a fact the pack does not give.

questionPlan.sample: Qantas Loyalty had 18.9m members and a 21.7% operating margin in FY26, against a Group Domestic margin of 13%, by the company's own figures. Which statement is supported?
questionPlan.answer: Loyalty earns more per dollar of revenue than domestic flying; the figures do not show whether rivals could copy it
choices: The loyalty program proves a sustained advantage, since a 21.7% margin could not survive imitation
Loyalty earns more per dollar of revenue than domestic flying; the figures do not show whether rivals could copy it
Qantas earns more in total from the program than from flying, since its margin is higher
questionPlan.why: A margin says nothing about imitability; third compares margins as if they were totals (the pack gives no loyalty-versus-flying profit totals).

questionPlan.sample: State the four VRIO questions in order and say what a 'no' at each one leaves the firm with.
questionPlan.answer: Self-rated: valuable (no: disadvantage); rare (no: parity); costly to imitate (no: temporary advantage); organised (no: unused advantage). Four yeses: sustained advantage.

lessons.title: Value chains and where profit sits
lessons.objective: Read a firm's margins by activity to say where along its chain the profit sits, what a margin does and does not measure, and what that suggests for strategy.

concepts.title: Value chain
concepts.summary: The sequence of activities a firm performs to design, produce, market, deliver and support its product.

concepts.title: Product margin and EBIT margin
concepts.summary: Product margin is revenue less the cost of the goods; EBIT margin also deducts operating costs such as wages and rent, so it is lower and closer to profit.

concepts.title: Supplier funding
concepts.summary: Payments suppliers make to retailers for promotions and services; the ACCC finds it contributes significantly to the chains' margins.

concepts.title: Segment margin
concepts.summary: The margin of one part of a firm, which shows where profit sits per dollar of revenue but not how much capital the part uses.

misconceptions: That a product margin is the retailer's profit. It leaves out operating costs; the ACCC says product margins generally exceed profit.
That a lower margin means a worse business. Metcash's much lower EBIT margin reflects being a wholesaler.
That a high margin segment is the biggest earner. A margin is a ratio; the pack gives no segment profit totals for Qantas beyond Loyalty EBIT.
That a retailer's margin comes only from selling more. The ACCC finds supplier funding contributes significantly.
sequence: The value chain as a map of activities (s6_vc_intro).
Grocery margins: product margin defined, why it exceeds profit, and EBIT as the better profit measure (s6_product_margin, s6_pm_vs_ebit, s6_coles_ebit, s6_ebit_stable).
Where the grocers' extra margin comes from: branded packaged goods, supplier funding and retail margin held in percentage terms (s6_branded_pl, s6_supplier_funding, s6_market_power).
A different link in the same chain: wholesaling earns less per dollar (s6_metcash_ebit).
Qantas as a chain inside one firm: Domestic 13%, International 4%, Loyalty 21.7% (s6_qan_segments, s5_qan_loyalty).
examples: ACCC: Coles EBIT margin 5.20% in 2023-24 as displayed, 5.04% on a 52-week basis (Coles' submission).
Qantas FY26: Loyalty revenue $2.9b and EBIT $625m (21.7% margin); Group Domestic margin 13%; Group International margin 4%.
ACCC: Coles and Woolworths sometimes accept a wholesale price rise only if the retail margin is held or raised in percentage terms.

figures.shows: Qantas FY26 by segment (Domestic, International, Loyalty): margin only; revenue and EBIT for Loyalty only, as the pack gives them.
figures.learnerAction: Rank the segments by margin, then list what the table does not tell you.

figures.shows: A grocery chain from grower to shopper with Metcash and the supermarkets marked and a callout at each link for the ACCC's finding about margin.
figures.learnerAction: Drag the margin labels to the link they describe.

questionPlan.sample: Qantas FY26: Group Domestic margin 13%, Group International margin 4%, Loyalty operating margin 21.7% on revenue of $2.9b. Which part earns the most per dollar of revenue, and what is the fair reading?
questionPlan.answer: Loyalty; per dollar of revenue it earns most, though the table does not show how much capital each part uses
choices: International, because it covers the most distance and so must earn the most per dollar
Loyalty; per dollar of revenue it earns most, though the table does not show how much capital each part uses
Domestic, because it is the largest part of the group and so earns the most per dollar of revenue
questionPlan.why: First and third bring in facts about size the table does not give.

questionPlan.sample: A news story says a supermarket makes a large margin on each product, so its profit must be just as large. What does the ACCC's explanation imply?
questionPlan.answer: Product margin omits wages, rent and other operating costs, so EBIT margin (about 5% for Coles, 2023-24) is the better guide
choices: The story is right, because product margin is the profit a retailer keeps from each product it sells
Margins cannot be compared across retailers, so neither measure tells you anything about profit
Product margin omits wages, rent and other operating costs, so EBIT margin (about 5% for Coles, 2023-24) is the better guide
questionPlan.why: First confuses the ratio with profit. Third over-corrects: comparisons are fine if the measure matches.

questionPlan.sample: The ACCC finds supplier funding for promotions is increasing and significantly contributes to Coles' and Woolworths' margins, and that they sometimes accept a wholesale price rise only if the retail margin is held or raised. What does this show about where the profit comes from?
questionPlan.answer: Part of it is paid by suppliers, which reflects the chains' bargaining position along the chain
choices: Part of it is paid by suppliers, which reflects the chains' bargaining position along the chain
It comes only from efficiency inside the stores, such as lower wage and rent costs per sale
It comes from shoppers alone, so suppliers are unaffected by the margins the chains earn
questionPlan.why: First and third leave out the supplier link the ACCC describes.

questionPlan.sample: Metcash's EBIT margins are much lower than Coles' and Woolworths'. Does that make it the weaker business?
questionPlan.answer: Not necessarily: the ACCC links the lower margin to wholesaling, so compare it with other wholesalers
choices: Yes, because a lower margin always means weaker management and a less valuable business
Not necessarily: the ACCC links the lower margin to wholesaling, so compare it with other wholesalers
No, because EBIT margin is not used to judge wholesalers, only retailers
questionPlan.why: Different links in the chain have different normal margins.

questionPlan.sample: About 70% of Qantas points are redeemed on Flight Rewards within the Group, and the Group claims over 35% of credit card spend in its program. A rival proposes to copy only the lounges. Which reading is best supported by the pack?
questionPlan.answer: The loyalty profit depends on the airline, since most points go on its own seats; copying one part may not copy the profit
choices: Loyalty can be copied separately, because points are only a currency and any firm can issue one
The lounges are the source of the loyalty margin, so a rival that builds lounges copies the profit
The loyalty profit depends on the airline, since most points go on its own seats; copying one part may not copy the profit
questionPlan.why: A judgement from two company figures; the pack does not test copying, so the answer is a reading, not a finding.

questionPlan.sample: Say what product margin and EBIT margin each leave in or out, and why the order of the two is not arbitrary.
questionPlan.answer: Self-rated: product margin = revenue less cost of goods; EBIT margin also deducts operating costs, so it is lower and nearer profit.

lessons.title: Network effects, platforms and lock-in
lessons.objective: Say whether a market is likely to tip toward one firm, which kind of network effect is at work, and how much customers are really tied in.

concepts.title: Network effect
concepts.summary: The value of a product depends on how many others use it; direct when users value other users, indirect when one group values the other.

concepts.title: Tipping
concepts.summary: One system pulls away from rivals once ahead; likelier when network benefits beat differentiation, multihoming is costly and switching is costly.

concepts.title: Two-sided platform
concepts.summary: An intermediary with two user groups, each valuing the other's presence; often subsidises one side to get both.

concepts.title: Switching cost and lock-in
concepts.summary: The costs of leaving a supplier, procedural, financial or relational; lock-in is when they are high enough to bind.

misconceptions: That network effects are the same as economies of scale. Scale lowers a firm's cost per unit; a network effect raises the value to each user.
That satisfied customers are locked in. The ACCC survey shows 92% happy with their mobile OS; that fits satisfaction as well as lock-in.
That every platform tips. Tipping needs costly multihoming and switching; app developers who can list on both stores weaken it.
That a loyalty program locks customers in. The ACCC finds low lock-in risk from free programs because members join several.
sequence: Define a network effect and the direct and indirect forms; separate it from scale economies (s7_ne_def, s7_ne_direct, s7_ne_not_scale); show critical mass and tipping with its three conditions (s7_critical, s7_tip, s7_tip_cond).

Two-sided markets: the definition, the subsidy and multihoming (s7_ts_def, s7_ts_subsidy, s7_multihome); Atlassian's Marketplace and Forge as a platform with outside developers (s7_atl_market, s7_atl_forge, s7_atl_ne).
What the ACCC says about digital markets: network effects, tipping and competition 'for the market' (s7_dpsi_char, s7_dpsi_tip).
Switching costs and lock-in defined (s7_sb_def, s7_lock_def), then the ACCC phone survey and the app-store overlap as evidence read for both (s7_dpsi_os, s7_dpsi_apps).
Cloud: high impediments to switching or multihoming, including egress fees (s7_dpsi_cloud).
Loyalty programs as lock-in: free programs low, paid programs likelier to bind (s7_loyalty_low, s7_loyalty_51, s7_loyalty_paid).
Why it matters for barriers: strong network effects lower the threat of entry (s7_porter_ne).
examples: ACCC survey (Australians aged 14+, Oct-Nov 2024): 92% happy with their mobile OS; 49% say a new OS would be hard to learn; 59% say friends and family use the same; 73% see no significant benefit in switching; 77% not likely to choose a different OS next time.
ACCC: around 90% or more of the top 100 apps in each of the App Store and Play Store are also on the other; 51% of grocery loyalty survey respondents belong to two or more programs.
Atlassian: Marketplace with thousands of third-party apps; Forge platform for developers.

figures.shows: Five products as rows with 'direct', 'indirect', 'scale economy' columns.
figures.learnerAction: Tick one column per product.

figures.shows: The ACCC survey percentages as five bars (92, 49, 59, 73, 77) with the question each answered; no interpretation.
figures.learnerAction: Mark each bar as 'fits satisfaction', 'fits lock-in' or 'both'.

questionPlan.sample: Sort each case into Direct network effect, Indirect (cross-side) network effect, or Scale economy. (1) A messaging app is more useful the more friends use it (invented). (2) More app developers make a phone more attractive to buyers and more buyers attract developers. (3) A bakery's cost per loaf falls as it bakes more (invented). (4) More third-party apps in the Atlassian Marketplace make its products more useful to customers, and more customers attract developers.
questionPlan.answer: Direct: 1. Indirect (cross-side): 2 and 4. Scale economy: 3.
questionPlan.why: Item 3 lowers the firm's cost, not raises users' value.

questionPlan.sample: In the ACCC survey 77% of Australians say they are unlikely to choose a phone with a different operating system next time. Is that evidence of lock-in?
questionPlan.answer: Not alone: it fits happiness too; the 49% who find a new OS hard and the 59% whose circle shares it point to switching costs
choices: Not alone: it fits happiness too; the 49% who find a new OS hard and the 59% whose circle shares it point to switching costs
Yes, because most people say they will not switch, and an unwillingness to switch is exactly what lock-in means
No, because 92% say they are happy with their phone, so lock-in cannot be any part of the explanation
questionPlan.why: First treats a behaviour as proof of cause. Third treats happiness as excluding lock-in.

questionPlan.sample: Around 90% or more of the top 100 apps in each of Apple's and Google's stores are available in the other. Which tipping condition does this weaken?
questionPlan.answer: That users and developers face high costs of multihoming
choices: That network benefits must exceed the value of differentiation
That switching costs must be high for consumers
That users and developers face high costs of multihoming
questionPlan.why: Developers listing on both stores shows multihoming is cheap on that side; the consumer-side evidence is separate.

questionPlan.sample: The ACCC finds the lock-in risk from free supermarket loyalty programs low, yet thinks paid subscription programs may bind more. Why?
questionPlan.answer: Free programs let members join several at no cost, while a fee discourages joining many and so concentrates spending
choices: Paid programs give larger discounts on every product, so members stay for the larger discount
Free programs let members join several at no cost, while a fee discourages joining many and so concentrates spending
Paid programs hold far more data about each member, so members cannot leave without losing value
questionPlan.why: The ACCC's reason is multihoming cost, not discount size or data.

questionPlan.sample: A new platform needs both buyers and sellers, and neither will come first. Microsoft's answer for its operating system was to discount the developer toolkit steeply. What is the logic?
questionPlan.answer: Subsidise the side whose presence attracts the other, and earn from the side that comes because of it
choices: Subsidise the side whose presence attracts the other, and earn from the side that comes because of it
Charge both sides the same price, so neither side feels unfairly treated and both join together
Wait until one side joins on its own, then price the other side's entry to match its value
questionPlan.why: First and third leave the chicken-and-egg problem unsolved.

questionPlan.sample: State the three conditions under which a market tips, and say which one the app-store overlap bears on.
questionPlan.answer: Self-rated: network utility exceeds differentiation; high multihoming cost; high switching cost. The overlap bears on multihoming cost.

lessons.title: Pricing strategy
lessons.objective: Judge which pricing approach fits a case, read what a firm's price pattern says about its position, and spot when a price is built to be hard to judge.

concepts.title: Value-based and cost-based pricing
concepts.summary: Value-based pricing sets price by what the customer will pay for the value; cost-based sets it from cost plus a margin.

concepts.title: Penetration and skimming
concepts.summary: Penetration starts low to win share fast and deter entry; skimming starts high to take early adopters' willingness to pay, then lowers.

concepts.title: Freemium
concepts.summary: A free base product with paid extras, which works where the cost of an extra free user is low.

concepts.title: Price discrimination
concepts.summary: Selling the same or similar goods at different prices to different segments.

concepts.title: High-low pricing
concepts.summary: Regular prices with regular periodic specials, which makes the 'real' price harder to judge.

misconceptions: That price should follow cost. Cost-based pricing suits firms with control of the market; value-based pricing follows what customers will pay.
That a low launch price always means a low long-run price. Penetration pricing is a way to win share and deter entry.
That points or specials are the same as a discount you can see. The ACCC finds points hide a discount of about 0.5c per $1 of spend.
That different prices for the same seat show unfairness only. They show segmentation by willingness to pay.
sequence: What pricing is for, and the two bases for setting it (s8_intro, s8_value, s8_cost_based).
Launch pricing: penetration against skimming and the entry-deterrence effect (s8_pen, s8_pen_barrier, s8_skim).

Free products: freemium and when its economics work, with Canva as the case (s8_freemium, s8_freemium_cost, s8_canva, s8_canva_users, s8_canva_edu), and Atlassian's transparent pricing (s8_atl_price).
Different prices for different buyers: the definition and the airline fare classes in the ACCC data (s8_pd, s8_air_fares).
Everyday low and high-low pricing in grocery: the cyclical specials and alternating cycles between Coles and Woolworths (s8_hilo, s8_hilo_alt) and the trouble of reference prices (s8_ref_price).
Points as a price: $2,000 of spending for a $10 discount (s8_points, s8_points_shortcut).
Tie back to networks: pricing to reach critical mass (s7_critical, s8_pen).
examples: ACCC: members of Coles' and Woolworths' loyalty programs need to spend $2,000 to earn a $10 discount, excluding bonus points: about 0.5c for every $1 spent.
ACCC: between June 2023 and June 2024, prices at one Coles and one Woolworths store in a common location moved in opposite directions about 12% of the time.
ACCC: real fares from January 2013 to January 2020 rose 41% (restricted economy), 26% (business) and 3% (discount economy).
Canva at the end of 2025: more than 265 million monthly active users and more than 31 million paid users.

figures.shows: Three price paths over time for a new product: penetration (low then rising), skimming (high then falling), freemium (zero base, paid tier). Axes only; no numbers.
figures.learnerAction: Match each path to a launch case.

figures.shows: The ACCC's three fare-class changes from 2013 to 2020 as bars, with the classes named and the changes unlabelled until the learner guesses the order.
figures.learnerAction: Order the classes by change, then read what the pattern suggests.

questionPlan.sample: The ACCC found that between June 2023 and June 2024 prices at one Coles and one Woolworths store in the same place moved in opposite directions about 12% of the time, with specials alternating. Which conclusion does that support?
questionPlan.answer: Shoppers face shifting reference prices, so judging a good deal is hard
choices: Coles and Woolworths agreed their specials in advance, so their prices move in step
Shoppers face shifting reference prices, so judging a good deal is hard
Every special is a real saving, because a price that falls is always below the usual price
questionPlan.why: First is not in the ACCC's finding; the ACCC reports the pattern and the difficulty it creates. Third ignores the concern about what the 'real' price is.

questionPlan.sample: ACCC: members need to spend $2,000 to earn a $10 discount, about 0.5c for every $1 spent. What does it show about points as a pricing tool?
questionPlan.answer: A small discount can be presented in a form shoppers find hard to value, so they may overvalue it
choices: Points are always a bad deal for shoppers, since the discount they earn is so small
Points raise the retailer's costs, so shelf prices must rise to pay for the program
A small discount can be presented in a form shoppers find hard to value, so they may overvalue it
questionPlan.why: First over-reads; the ACCC says people may not do the calculation. Third is not in the source.

questionPlan.sample: A new messaging app needs many users before it is useful. Which launch price fits, and why?
questionPlan.answer: A low or free launch price, to reach critical mass and discourage rivals
choices: A high launch price, to take the most from early adopters before any rival appears
A low or free launch price, to reach critical mass and discourage rivals
A price set at cost plus a fixed margin, so every user pays what serving them costs
questionPlan.why: First is skimming, which suits low price sensitivity and a protected position. Third ignores that the value depends on others using it.

questionPlan.sample: Canva offers a free base product and charges for more features; by the end of 2025 it reported more than 265 million monthly active users and more than 31 million paid users. What must be true for freemium to work?
questionPlan.answer: Serving an extra free user costs little, and enough free users move to paid
choices: Free users must outnumber paid users by a fixed ratio, or the free tier will not pay for itself
The free product must be supported by advertising, since free users bring no other revenue
Serving an extra free user costs little, and enough free users move to paid
questionPlan.why: First and third are not conditions in the source; the source names low marginal cost and avoiding cannibalisation.

questionPlan.sample: From 2013 to 2020 real fares for restricted economy rose 41%, for business 26% and for discount economy 3% (ACCC). The airlines sell similar seats at different prices to different segments. What is that pricing strategy called?
questionPlan.answer: Price discrimination (accept 'differential pricing' or 'segment pricing')

questionPlan.sample: Say when you would pick penetration pricing and when skimming, in one sentence each.
questionPlan.answer: Self-rated: penetration to reach many customers quickly, deter entry and start word of mouth; skimming where early customers will pay more and the firm needs to recoup sunk costs.

lessons.title: Diversification and acquisition
lessons.objective: Judge a move into a new business with the three tests, say when a diversified group is worth more together than apart, and read a portfolio's history as strategy.

concepts.title: The four growth directions
concepts.summary: Market penetration, market development, product development and diversification, in rising order of risk.

concepts.title: Three tests for diversification
concepts.summary: Is the industry attractive, can the cost of entry be recouped, and will the new unit and the firm each be better off.

concepts.title: Related and unrelated diversification
concepts.summary: Related moves share value-chain links with the existing business; research cited by Morris and Tripathi finds they do better.

concepts.title: Conglomerate discount
concepts.summary: The tendency for a diversified group to be worth less than its parts, because investors can diversify themselves.

concepts.title: Portfolio renewal
concepts.summary: Buying and selling businesses over time, so the group's mix changes.

misconceptions: That diversification reduces risk and therefore always creates value. Investors can diversify themselves, so a group must add value beyond that.
That a new market is just another place to sell. Diversification means uncharted territory and the firm may lack the skills.
That a group's mix is fixed. Fertiliser was about 55% of Wesfarmers' profit at listing and is about 1% now.
That a failed entry proves the industry was bad. Masters lost over $3.2 billion partly because product schedules followed northern hemisphere seasons.
sequence: Open on Masters: Woolworths' 2009 plan to enter hardware, long dominated by Bunnings, 150 stores in five years (s9_masters_intro, s12_masters_late).
The four growth directions and why diversification is riskiest (s9_ansoff_pen, s9_ansoff); the three tests (s9_tests).
Apply the tests to Masters: losses, localisation and the exit (s9_masters_fail, s9_masters_2015, s9_masters_close).
Why conglomerates exist and why investors discount them (s9_cong_adv, s9_cong_dis, s9_cong_dis2); related against unrelated (s9_related).

Wesfarmers' own account: a diversified portfolio, the capital allocation avenues, and acquire or divest where long-term value rises (s9_wes_div, s9_wes_q, s9_wes_alloc, s9_wes_acq, s9_wes_cap, s9_wes_fert).
The same portfolio's history: bought Coles in 2007 for $22 billion, spun it off in 2018 (s9_coles_buy, s9_coles_spin). The pack gives no reasons for the spin-off.
examples: Masters: announced 25 August 2009 with a plan for 150 stores in five years; losses over $3.2 billion over seven years; all stores closed by 11 December 2016; a loss of $227.4 million in 2015.
Wesfarmers FY26: NPAT $2.9 billion; 'a diversified portfolio, where weakness in one business may be compensated by strong performances in other businesses'.
Invented, labelled: a supermarket chain weighing an online delivery arm against buying a hotel group.

figures.shows: Three tests as rows and five pieces of Masters evidence as cards.
figures.learnerAction: Drag each card to the test it informs.

figures.shows: Wesfarmers' portfolio from the share of fertiliser at listing (about 55% of profit) to now (about 1%), with Coles bought in 2007 and spun off in 2018.
figures.learnerAction: Mark each event as buying, selling or reshaping; the reasons are hidden because the pack does not give them.

questionPlan.sample: Sort each piece of Masters evidence under the test it most informs: Attractiveness, Cost of entry or Better off. (1) Hardware had long been dominated by Bunnings. (2) The plan was 150 stores in five years. (3) Product schedules followed northern hemisphere seasons. (4) The chair said it would take years to become profitable and the losses could not be sustained. (5) The stores borrowed the format of conventional Lowe's stores.
questionPlan.answer: Attractiveness: 1. Cost of entry: 2 and 4. Better off: 3 and 5.
questionPlan.why: Items 3 and 5 show the parent's know-how not giving a usable advantage in Australia.

questionPlan.sample: Wesfarmers' chair says a diversified portfolio means weakness in one business may be compensated by strength in another. Why might investors still discount a conglomerate?
questionPlan.answer: Investors can diversify themselves by holding several shares, so the group has to add value beyond spreading risk
choices: Investors can diversify themselves by holding several shares, so the group has to add value beyond spreading risk
Because diversified firms are always badly run, as no manager can run unrelated businesses well
Because diversified firms pay no dividends, since they keep all cash to fund new ventures
questionPlan.why: First and third are not in the source.

questionPlan.sample: Fertiliser contributed about 55% of Wesfarmers' profit at listing and about 1% now, the chair writes. What does that show?
questionPlan.answer: The group's mix has been renewed over time rather than held fixed
choices: That fertiliser was a failed business that the group had to shrink and then give up
The group's mix has been renewed over time rather than held fixed
That Wesfarmers has shrunk, because a business that once earned 55% now earns almost nothing
questionPlan.why: First needs reasons the chair does not give. Third: the report gives revenue of $47.3b and NPAT of $2.9b.

questionPlan.sample: A supermarket chain is weighing an online delivery arm against buying a hotel group (both invented). Which is likelier to pass the better-off test, using the research cited by Morris and Tripathi?
questionPlan.answer: The delivery arm, because it shares customers, suppliers and logistics with the grocery business
choices: The hotel group, because a larger and more different market gives more room to spread risk
Both equally, because diversification of any kind spreads risk and so passes the test
The delivery arm, because it shares customers, suppliers and logistics with the grocery business
questionPlan.why: First mistakes distance for diversification benefit. Third repeats the risk-spreading fallacy.

questionPlan.sample: Sort each invented move into the Ansoff direction it represents: Market penetration, Market development, Product development or Diversification. (1) A bakery chain opens more shops in cities where it already trades. (2) The same chain takes its shops to a new state. (3) The chain adds a coffee range for its current customers. (4) The chain buys a hotel.
questionPlan.answer: 1 Market penetration; 2 Market development; 3 Product development; 4 Diversification.
questionPlan.why: Direction depends on whether the product, the market or both are new.

questionPlan.sample: State the three tests for a diversification move and name the one Masters' product schedules most clearly failed.
questionPlan.answer: Self-rated: attractiveness, cost of entry, better off. Masters' seasonal schedules point to better off.

lessons.title: Make or buy
lessons.objective: Judge whether a firm should do an activity itself or contract it, using scale, alternatives, control and the cost of getting it wrong.

concepts.title: Vertical integration
concepts.summary: Owning more links of the chain: backward toward suppliers, forward toward customers.

concepts.title: Outsourcing
concepts.summary: Contracting an activity to another firm, usually a non-core one, in exchange for lower cost or specialist capability and less control.

concepts.title: The scale test
concepts.summary: Integration needs enough volume to justify the capital, as Drakes' distribution centre shows.

concepts.title: Credible bypass
concepts.summary: A buyer's real option to supply itself constrains its supplier's pricing even when it is not used on most lines.

concepts.title: Hold-up
concepts.summary: Once one side has invested in a specialised asset, the other can bargain it down.

misconceptions: That owning the supplier gives control for free. Integration needs capital and can move a firm into a business it does not know.
That outsourcing is always cheaper. A Deloitte survey in 2005 reported that a quarter of firms which had outsourced reversed their strategy.
That if one large buyer can integrate, all can. The ACCC says few independents have Drakes' scale.
That a supplier with large share has unlimited pricing power. A credible bypass limits it.
sequence: Define the two directions of integration (s10_vi, s10_vi_back, s10_vi_fwd) and set out the gains and the costs (s10_vi_gains, s10_vi_losses, s10_vi_large; Morris and Tripathi on power and skills: s10_morris_vi).

Drakes: a $125m distribution centre in Adelaide, why few could copy it, the effect on Metcash, and the continuing Queensland supply (s10_drakes, s10_drakes_scale, s10_drakes_impact, s10_drakes_constraint, s10_drakes_qld).
Why independents rarely go direct to suppliers (s10_metcash_scale) and why fresh produce differs from packaged lines (s3_metcash_74, s3_metcash_fresh).
The other side: outsourcing, Drucker's slogan, why firms do it and why a quarter reversed (s10_drucker, s10_reasons, s10_reversal, s10_own_control).
Hold-up and transaction cost in a short case (s10_tc); Qantas' 2020 ground-handling outsourcing at ten airports as the real example of a contracted function (s10_qan_ground).
examples: Drakes: 68 stores, $125 million distribution centre opened in Adelaide on 26 September 2019, still supplied by Metcash in Queensland to at least 3 June 2029 (ACCC).
Metcash: about 74% of IGA purchases go through it; IGA stores source 50 to 90% of fresh groceries elsewhere.
Qantas outsourced ground handling at ten Australian airports in 2020, affecting about 1,800 employees (Wikipedia).

figures.shows: A two-column list: 'favours doing it yourself' and 'favours contracting', with ten reasons from the Wikipedia lists to place.
figures.learnerAction: Drag each reason to a column.

figures.shows: A chain from supplier to Metcash to IGA stores with Drakes marked as having stepped around Metcash in South Australia only.
figures.learnerAction: Mark where scale is needed and where it is not.

questionPlan.sample: The ACCC says few independent supermarket groups could replicate Drakes' move to supply itself. Why?
questionPlan.answer: Drakes is among the largest independents, so it had the volume to justify a distribution centre
choices: Other independents lack the ambition to build a distribution centre of their own
Drakes is among the largest independents, so it had the volume to justify a distribution centre
Metcash blocks independents from leaving by tying them to long supply contracts
questionPlan.why: First and third are not in the source.

questionPlan.sample: Drakes supplies itself in South Australia and still buys from Metcash in Queensland. What does the South Australian move do to Metcash even where Drakes stays a customer?
questionPlan.answer: It shows that a customer can bypass the supplier, which constrains Metcash's wholesale pricing
choices: It shows that a customer can bypass the supplier, which constrains Metcash's wholesale pricing
Nothing, since Drakes stayed a Metcash customer in Queensland and Metcash lost only part of its trade
It forces Metcash to close its Queensland distribution centre, since Drakes was its anchor customer
questionPlan.why: The ACCC says the ability to bypass 'may provide a realistic constraint'; third is not in the source.

questionPlan.sample: IGA stores buy about 74% of what they stock through Metcash but source 50 to 90% of fresh groceries elsewhere. Which pattern of make-or-buy does it show?
questionPlan.answer: They use the wholesaler where its scale and range matter, and go elsewhere where alternatives are many
choices: They integrate fresh produce and outsource packaged goods, since they own the stores that sell both
They outsource everything, because small stores cannot afford to run any supply activity themselves
They use the wholesaler where its scale and range matter, and go elsewhere where alternatives are many
questionPlan.why: The pack describes purchasing, not integration, for IGA stores.

questionPlan.sample: Sort each into Favours doing it yourself or Favours contracting it out. (1) Lower transaction costs. (2) Access to world-class capabilities. (3) Capture of upstream or downstream profit margins. (4) Higher costs of switching to other suppliers or buyers. (5) Weaker motivation for good performance at the start of the chain. (6) Freeing internal resources for other purposes.
questionPlan.answer: Doing it yourself: 1 and 3. Contracting out: 2, 4, 5 and 6.
questionPlan.why: Items 4 and 5 are costs of integrating, so they favour contracting.

questionPlan.sample: A 2005 Deloitte survey found a quarter of firms which had outsourced tasks reversed their strategy. What does that suggest for an outsourcing decision?
questionPlan.answer: That early savings can be offset by later costs in coordination and control, so price alone is not the test
choices: That early savings can be offset by later costs in coordination and control, so price alone is not the test
That outsourcing never saves money, since a quarter of the firms that tried it went back to doing the work themselves
That reversal shows the original plan was well made and was simply completed
questionPlan.why: First over-generalises. Third misreads reversal as success.

questionPlan.sample: Give two reasons a firm might make rather than buy, and two it might buy rather than make.
questionPlan.answer: Self-rated: make for control, margin capture, lower transaction cost, protection from supplier power; buy for scale, specialist capability, focus, flexibility.

lessons.title: Disruption and the incumbent's dilemma
lessons.objective: Say whether an entrant is a disruptor, explain why a well-run incumbent may rationally ignore it, and judge the incumbent's possible responses.

concepts.title: Sustaining innovation
concepts.summary: Improvement that serves the incumbent's best customers with a better version of what they already buy.

concepts.title: Low-end disruption
concepts.summary: A good-enough product that wins the customers the incumbent finds least profitable and then moves up.

concepts.title: New-market disruption
concepts.summary: A product for customers the incumbent does not serve at all.

concepts.title: The incumbent's dilemma
concepts.summary: A well-managed firm can do everything right for its best customers and still lose, because the early disruptive market is small and unprofitable.

concepts.title: Cannibalising yourself
concepts.summary: Replacing your own profitable product before an entrant does.

misconceptions: That disruption means any new technology. Not every revolutionary innovation is disruptive.
That incumbents fail because they are lazy or ignore technology. The 'technology mudslide' view is wrong on the source's account; Kodak invested in digital.
That the theory explains everything. The article cites critics who say it is oversold, with named victims still dominant.
That the response is to cut price. The pack's cases are a separate low-cost unit (Jetstar) and ending your own legacy product (Atlassian Data Center).
sequence: Define disruptive innovation and separate it from sustaining innovation (s11_def, s11_not_all, s11_mudslide); note the critics (s11_critic).

The two forms: low-end and new-market (s11_lowend, s11_newmarket) and why the dilemma arises: small deals, low early profit, scarce resources (s11_outsiders, s11_incumbent_deals, s11_simple, s11_ignore, s11_dilemma, s11_morris_dis).
Kodak: invented the digital camera, led US digital camera sales by 2005, and still lost its profit base; the misconception corrected (s11_kodak_invented, s11_kodak_myth, s11_kodak_ez).
Blockbuster: the online service that its own franchisees said undercut their stores (s11_blockbuster_cause, s11_blockbuster_online, s11_blockbuster_au).
Responses: Qantas answers Virgin Blue with Jetstar (s11_jetstar_response, s11_jetstar_threat); Atlassian ends sale of its Data Center product (s11_dc).
Schumpeter's creative destruction as the wider frame (s11_morris_cd).
examples: Kodak: 'first self-contained digital camera prototype in the mid-1970s'; in 2005 No. 1 in US digital camera sales at $5.7 billion.
Atlassian: no new Data Center sales to new customers from March 2026; term licences and expansions end March 2028; maintenance and support end March 2029.
Qantas: Jetstar created in 2001 after Virgin Blue's entry took share.

figures.shows: Six entrants described by who they serve and how their product compares, with sustaining, low-end and new-market as the three answers.
figures.learnerAction: Classify each, then see which cases the lesson used.

figures.shows: Blockbuster 2004 to 2010: online service launch, Total Access, franchisee lawsuit, bankruptcy; no commentary until the learner places each.
figures.learnerAction: Mark each as a move that served the old model or the new one.

questionPlan.sample: Sort each invented entrant into Sustaining, Low-end disruption or New-market disruption. (1) A faster version of the market leader's top camera for its best customers. (2) A cheap, simple camera that the leader's lowest-margin buyers find good enough. (3) A camera in a phone, for people who did not buy cameras at all. (4) A better lens for the leader's professional customers.
questionPlan.answer: Sustaining: 1 and 4. Low-end: 2. New-market: 3.
questionPlan.why: Sustaining innovation improves what the best customers already buy; the disruptive forms start where the incumbent is not looking.

questionPlan.sample: A commentator says Kodak failed because it refused to invest in digital cameras. What does the Wikipedia article say?
questionPlan.answer: Kodak built the first digital camera prototype and led US digital camera sales by 2005; the trouble was the transition
choices: The commentator is right: Kodak refused to invest in digital cameras and never built one of its own
Kodak built the first digital camera prototype and led US digital camera sales by 2005; the trouble was the transition
Kodak failed only because Fujifilm took its film customers; digital cameras played no part in it
questionPlan.why: The article calls the refusal story a common misconception. Third omits the digital transition.

questionPlan.sample: Blockbuster's franchisees sued in 2007 saying its online service and Total Access plan undercut their stores. What does that show about responding to a new model?
questionPlan.answer: The new model competed with the firm's own existing channel, so responding hurt part of the old business
choices: The online service was a bad idea, since customers never wanted rentals delivered by mail
Franchisees were not allowed to sell online, so the lawsuit was about the franchise agreement alone
The new model competed with the firm's own existing channel, so responding hurt part of the old business
questionPlan.why: First needs a judgement the source does not make. Third is not in the source.

questionPlan.sample: After Virgin Blue's entry took share, Qantas created Jetstar in 2001 as a separate low-cost brand. What does that illustrate?
questionPlan.answer: An incumbent can answer a low-priced entrant with a separate unit rather than discounting its main brand
choices: An incumbent can answer a low-priced entrant with a separate unit rather than discounting its main brand
That Qantas gave up its full-service position and moved the whole airline to low fares
That price wars always favour the incumbent, so Qantas won by cutting fares across its network
questionPlan.why: Qantas kept the Qantas brand; the ACCC calls it a dual brand strategy. The pack does not call Virgin Blue a disruptor, so the fit with the theory is a reading.

questionPlan.sample: Atlassian announced in September 2025 that it would end sales of Data Center to new customers from March 2026, end term licences and expansions in March 2028 and end support in March 2029. Which dilemma is it facing?
questionPlan.answer: Whether to retire its own profitable product before a rival does, at the risk that customers who cannot move leave
choices: Whether to enter a new market with an existing product, at the risk of overreaching its skills
Whether to retire its own profitable product before a rival does, at the risk that customers who cannot move leave
Whether to outsource Data Center to a partner, at the risk of losing control of the product
questionPlan.why: The 10-K itself names the risk to customers who cannot migrate; the pack does not say rivals forced the move.

questionPlan.sample: Explain in two sentences why a well-run incumbent might rationally ignore a disruptive entrant at first.
