questionPlan.answer: Self-rated: the early market is small and unprofitable against the incumbent's expectations, and chasing it would divert resources from sustaining the customers who pay the bills.

lessons.title: First movers and price wars
lessons.objective: Judge whether being first will give a lasting edge, and whether to match a rival's price cut.

concepts.title: First-mover advantage
concepts.summary: The edge gained by the first significant occupant of a segment, from technology leadership, control of resources or buyer switching costs.

concepts.title: Second-mover advantage
concepts.summary: Followers learn from the first mover's costs and mistakes, and sometimes overtake it.

concepts.title: Price war
concepts.summary: Repeated cutting of prices below rivals', which can become unsustainable.

concepts.title: Promotion against cut
concepts.summary: A short-term special is not a long-term price change; mistaking one for the other can start a war.

misconceptions: That first always wins. First movers often fail, and profits can fall near zero as patents expire.
That a new entrant that succeeded was a first mover. Virgin Blue entered after Qantas and Ansett and benefited from Ansett's collapse.
That every rival price cut must be matched. The first step is to check whether it is a short promotion.
That quiet rivalry between two airlines proves agreement. The ACCC reports they were content with their shares, not that they agreed.
sequence: Define first-mover advantage and its three sources (s12_fma, s12_mech, s12_switch); then its limits and the second-mover case (s12_disad, s12_duration, s12_second, s12_conclude).

Virgin Blue's entry: luck of timing and terminal access, not first-mover advantage (s12_virgin_entry); ALDI and Bonza as later entrants who took years or must grow much more (s12_aldi_2001, s12_bonza, s3_aldi_20).
Price wars: definition, causes, and what to do first (s12_pw_def, s12_pw_causes, s12_pw_react, s12_pw_options, s12_pw_effects).
Cases: Kodak and Fuji (s12_kodak_fuji); Qantas and Virgin in the early 2010s and after (s12_air_pw, s12_air_tiger, s12_qan_shares); the grocery cycles of specials (s8_hilo_alt).
examples: Kodak: revenue fell from $15.97 billion in 1996 to $14.36 billion in 1997 and net earnings from $1.29 billion to $5 million, the year a price war with Fuji began (Wikipedia; the article attributes the profit fall to the war but gives no breakdown).
Qantas and Virgin: about 2/3 and 1/3 of domestic passengers as their publicly talked-about targets (ACCC).
Virgin Blue: began 31 August 2000; Ansett failed September 2001.

figures.shows: First-mover mechanisms (three) as columns with five cases as rows, with a 'none' option.
figures.learnerAction: Tick the mechanism that applies to each case.

figures.shows: Domestic airline competition: Virgin Blue's entry, Jetstar created, Ansett fails, price war, content years.
figures.learnerAction: Mark moves as first, follower or reaction.

questionPlan.sample: Sort each case into the first-mover mechanism it shows: Technology leadership, Control of resources, Buyer switching costs or None of these. (1) The first restaurant of a new type takes the best sites in town. (2) A first mover cuts unit cost and so holds an absolute cost advantage. (3) Customers stay with the first brand they met that performed. (4) A firm is first to announce a product but never ships it.
questionPlan.answer: Control of resources: 1. Technology leadership: 2. Buyer switching costs: 3. None: 4.
questionPlan.why: Item 4 is not a market occupant at all.

questionPlan.sample: A manager says being first guarantees a lasting edge. Which evidence best answers her?
questionPlan.answer: First movers carry heavy development costs and profits can fall as patents expire, so followers sometimes overtake
choices: First movers always have the lowest costs, because they move first down the experience curve
First movers carry heavy development costs and profits can fall as patents expire, so followers sometimes overtake
Followers always win, because they learn from the first mover's mistakes at no cost to themselves
questionPlan.why: First and third are the two simple extremes; the source says studies differ.

questionPlan.sample: Virgin Blue launched in 2000 after the incumbents; Ansett collapsed in 2001 and Virgin took terminal space it would otherwise lack. What does that say about the source of Virgin's position?
questionPlan.answer: Partly timing and access to scarce terminal space after the incumbent failed, not only being early
choices: First-mover advantage, since it was the first low-cost airline in the Australian market
Pure luck, since its low-cost formula and its aircraft choices played no part in its growth
Partly timing and access to scarce terminal space after the incumbent failed, not only being early
questionPlan.why: Virgin followed Qantas and Ansett, so it was not first. Third ignores its low-cost formula.

questionPlan.sample: Woolworths puts a product on special for two weeks and the ACCC finds Coles and Woolworths specials alternate in cycles. Should Coles cut its everyday price in reply?
questionPlan.answer: Not yet: first check whether it is a short promotion in a regular cycle, because matching could start a price war
choices: Not yet: first check whether it is a short promotion in a regular cycle, because matching could start a price war
Yes, straight away, to protect its share before shoppers learn to buy the special elsewhere
No, because specials never move sales, so there is nothing to protect by responding
questionPlan.why: First is the common reflex. Third is wrong: the question is what response is warranted.

questionPlan.sample: The ACCC reports Qantas and Virgin fought for share in the early 2010s, abandoned it after significant losses, and later were 'content with their respective shares', publicly talking of 2/3 and 1/3. Which reading is best supported?
questionPlan.answer: Both had found that matching each other's cuts hurt both; the ACCC does not claim they agreed
choices: They secretly agreed shares between themselves, which is why the price war ended
Both had found that matching each other's cuts hurt both; the ACCC does not claim they agreed
Price competition ended because customers stopped caring about fares after the pandemic
questionPlan.why: First asserts what the ACCC does not. Third is not in the source.

questionPlan.sample: List the four reactions to a long-term price cut in the source and say which one the lesson says to try after checking the cut is real.
questionPlan.answer: Self-rated: reduce price, maintain price, split the market, or react with other measures such as quality or promotion.

lessons.title: Strategy under uncertainty
lessons.objective: Choose the uncertainties that should drive a set of scenarios and judge when staging a commitment (a real option) is worth its cost.

concepts.title: Scenario planning
concepts.summary: Telling plausible, contrasting stories about the future to test a strategy, not forecasting one.

concepts.title: The official future
concepts.summary: A straight-line projection that ignores qualitative change.

concepts.title: Real option
concepts.summary: The right, not the obligation, to defer, expand, abandon or stage a commitment; most valuable when uncertainty is high and management can act.

concepts.title: Option premium
concepts.summary: The upfront cost of keeping the flexibility.

misconceptions: That scenarios predict. They prepare; a single scenario is unlikely.
That flexibility is free. Real options have a premium, and waiting can let a rival move first.
That evidence shows scenarios pay. The source says evidence is anecdotal and mostly from Shell.
That a diversified or flexible firm avoids shocks. Qantas still took about a $420 million hit from the 2026 fuel spike, by its own figure.
sequence: Define scenario planning and the 'official future' (s13_scen_def, s13_official); Shell, Wack and the critics (s13_shell, s13_crafting, s13_critic, s13_evidence).
Define real options and when they matter (s13_ro_def, s13_ro_when); the three examples: expand, abandon, defer (s13_expand, s13_abandon, s13_defer).
A company in a shock: Qantas' FY26 response when fuel prices escalated in the Middle East conflict (s13_qan_fuel); Virgin's wet leases as a flexible way to serve regional routes (s13_virgin_wet).
Masters again, as a commitment to 150 stores in five years that staging might have changed (s12_masters_late, s9_masters_fail).
Wesfarmers' longer bets, without claims about how they are staged (s13_wes_options).
examples: Qantas FY26: net impact of about $420 million on 2H26 pre-tax profit from the Middle East conflict; actions included redeploying capacity, raising fares, cutting domestic capacity, pre-funding debt, pausing the buy-back, cutting capex and restructuring hedging.
Shell: scenario planning developed by Pierre Wack from 1971 and given impetus by the oil shock two years later (Wikipedia).
Masters: plan announced 2009 for 150 stores in five years.

figures.shows: A two-by-two with two uncertainties on the axes for a fictional regional airline and four scenario names left blank.
figures.learnerAction: Choose which two of six uncertainties go on the axes, then name the four cells.

figures.shows: Three ways to enter a market (commit fully, stage, wait), with cost of waiting, cost of the option and what is learned.
figures.learnerAction: Fill each cell in words.

questionPlan.sample: A fictional regional airline is building scenarios. Sort each factor into Driving uncertainty (matters a lot and could go either way), Predetermined (will happen regardless) or Minor detail. (1) Whether fuel prices stay elevated. (2) Whether a second low-cost carrier survives. (3) The airline's logo colours. (4) Fuel and crews will be needed whichever scenario occurs.
questionPlan.answer: Driving uncertainty: 1 and 2. Predetermined: 4. Minor detail: 3.
questionPlan.why: Item 4 sits in every scenario so it cannot separate them.

questionPlan.sample: When fuel prices escalated, Qantas says it redeployed capacity to international spillover traffic, cut domestic capacity, raised fares, paused the buy-back and restructured hedging, crediting a multi-gauge fleet. Which description fits best?
questionPlan.answer: Flexibility that had been built earlier let it respond, though the shock still cost about $420 million
choices: Proof that flexibility removes shocks, since Qantas protected its profit in full from the fuel spike
A forecast that fuel prices would rise, which Qantas used to plan the response in advance
Flexibility that had been built earlier let it respond, though the shock still cost about $420 million
questionPlan.why: The figure is the company's; first ignores the cost, third confuses a response with a forecast.

questionPlan.sample: A retailer can open 20 stores now or open 3 and expand if sales pass a threshold (both invented). What does staging buy and cost?
questionPlan.answer: It keeps the option to expand after learning, at the cost of a slower start and the risk a rival moves first
choices: It keeps the option to expand after learning, at the cost of a slower start and the risk a rival moves first
It costs nothing and is always better, because information about demand is free to collect
It is only useful when the outcome is certain, since an uncertain market needs full commitment
questionPlan.why: Real options are most valuable when uncertainty is high; the premium here is the delay and its competitive risk.

questionPlan.sample: Woolworths announced in 2009 a plan for 150 Masters stores in five years, and the venture later lost over $3.2 billion, partly because product schedules followed northern hemisphere seasons. What might staging have changed? (A reasoned hypothetical.)
questionPlan.answer: Fewer stores first would have exposed the seasonal mismatch before the rest were committed, at the cost of a slower start
choices: It would have guaranteed a profit, since a smaller number of stores is always easier to run well
Fewer stores first would have exposed the seasonal mismatch before the rest were committed, at the cost of a slower start
Nothing, because Masters was a sound idea and the chain failed only through bad luck in the market
questionPlan.why: The pack states the plan and the failure; the counterfactual is the learner's reasoning, not a fact.

questionPlan.sample: Wikipedia says the evidence for scenario planning is anecdotal and mostly from Shell. What follows for a manager?
questionPlan.answer: Use scenarios to challenge assumptions and prepare, and do not treat them as proof they will pay
choices: Never use scenarios, because evidence that they work is anecdotal and so proves nothing
Choose the most likely scenario and plan for it alone, which is the aim of the method
Use scenarios to challenge assumptions and prepare, and do not treat them as proof they will pay
questionPlan.why: First over-reacts; third is the 'official future' trap in another form.

questionPlan.sample: Name four kinds of real option and say what the 'premium' is for one of them.
questionPlan.answer: Self-rated: defer, expand, contract, abandon, stage, growth. The premium is the extra upfront cost of keeping the flexibility.

lessons.title: Why good plans fail
lessons.objective: Diagnose why a plan failed from a case: a mismatch with the market, an organisation that did not carry it out, or a plan that was not revised as the world changed.

concepts.title: Implementation
concepts.summary: Aligning people, processes and systems with the strategy.

concepts.title: Strategic drift
concepts.summary: Gradual change that is not noticed until it is too late (Handy).

concepts.title: Alignment of systems
concepts.summary: Targets, measurement, planning and pay that point at the same objective, as Wesfarmers describes.

concepts.title: Emergence
concepts.summary: The weight of what is learned along the way rises as the environment gets harder to forecast.

misconceptions: That a failed plan shows planning is useless. A 2019 meta-analysis of nearly 9,000 organisations found planning has a positive average effect, but having a plan is not enough.
That failure is always bad execution. Some plans fail because they do not fit the market, as Masters' seasons suggest.
That a strategy, once set, guides changes. Mintzberg's view: once established it can resist change.
That measures do not matter. Wesfarmers ties systems to return on investment, not to asset or revenue growth.
sequence: What goes wrong between plan and result: strategy excludes signals, resists change, and implementation is alignment (s14_limits, s14_impl, s14_iter).
Drift and success as a trap: Handy's strategic drift and Pascale's 'nothing fails like success' (s14_drift, s14_pascale).
The evidence on planning (s14_evidence) and how emergence grows with volatility (s1_emergent).

Cases: Masters (s14_masters_fail, s14_masters_diff, s14_masters_cairns), Kodak's diversification attempts (s14_kodak_div, s14_kodak_plan), Blockbuster's franchisee conflict (s14_blockbuster_franchise), Coles' culture and deferred plans (s14_coles_culture, s14_coles_deferred).
The counter-case: Wesfarmers' account of aligning systems to a financial objective (s14_wes_align, s14_wes_fin).
examples: Masters: plan for 150 stores in five years, brightly lit stores with call buzzers and a focus on female shoppers, losses over $3.2 billion in seven years.
Kodak: large budgets for diversification with little long-term planning or help from outside experts; later strategy shifts.
Wesfarmers: more than 100,000 team members; target setting, management accounting, planning and pay aligned to return on investment.

figures.shows: Five failure cases as rows (Masters; Kodak diversification; Blockbuster franchise; Coles' deferred rebrand; Handy's drift) with three diagnosis columns.
figures.learnerAction: Place each case in one column.

figures.shows: A loop of analyse, plan, act and learn, with the places where a plan can break marked.
figures.learnerAction: Mark where each case broke.

questionPlan.sample: Sort each case by the best diagnosis: Plan did not fit the market, Organisation did not carry it out, or Plan was not revised as the world changed. (1) Masters' product schedules followed northern hemisphere seasons. (2) Kodak's diversification ventures had large budgets but little long-term planning and little help from outside experts. (3) Blockbuster's franchisees sued over its online service. (4) An independent report criticised the culture at Coles in 2007. (5) A gradual change goes unnoticed until it is too late (strategic drift).
questionPlan.answer: Did not fit the market: 1. Did not carry it out: 2, 3 and 4. Not revised: 5.
questionPlan.why: Items 2 to 4 point at the organisation; item 5 is the textbook case of an unrevised plan.

questionPlan.sample: Wesfarmers' chair says alignment needs target setting, management accounting, measurement, reporting, planning and pay to be built around return on investment, not asset or revenue growth. Which setup shows that alignment?
questionPlan.answer: Division targets and bonuses based on return on capital, so managers weigh investments by their return
choices: A mission statement displayed in every store and read out at the start of each shift
Division targets and bonuses based on return on capital, so managers weigh investments by their return
Bonuses based on revenue growth, which rewards managers who add sales to the group

questionPlan.sample: Wikipedia reports a 2019 meta-analysis of nearly 9,000 organisations that found strategic planning has a positive impact on performance, but having a plan is not enough. What follows?
questionPlan.answer: Planning helps on average, but how it is done matters, so one plan's failure does not show planning is useless
choices: Planning always works, so a plan that fails must have been carried out badly by its owners
Planning is a waste, since plans so often fail and the firms that plan are no better off
Planning helps on average, but how it is done matters, so one plan's failure does not show planning is useless
questionPlan.why: First ignores the caveat; third ignores the average effect.

questionPlan.sample: A plan worked for ten years. Competitors then changed and the firm kept to the plan until results fell. Which advice fits the sources?
questionPlan.answer: Treat strategy as learning: make modest probes and revise on feedback
choices: Treat strategy as learning: make modest probes and revise on feedback
Hold the plan, since changing it in response to rivals shows weakness to staff and investors
Drop planning altogether, since a plan that worked for ten years proves nothing about the next
questionPlan.why: First is the trap Pascale and Mintzberg describe. Third discards the planning evidence.

questionPlan.sample: Which firm should plan in the greatest detail: one in a stable environment or one in a volatile market? (Morris and Tripathi.)
questionPlan.answer: The one in a stable environment, because the role of emergence grows as the environment becomes volatile
choices: The one in a volatile market, because it faces more change and so needs the most detailed plan
The one in a stable environment, because the role of emergence grows as the environment becomes volatile
Both equally, because the amount of planning depends on the size of the firm and not its environment
questionPlan.why: The book gives postal services and the Catholic Church as stable examples.
